steps.do: List the project layout to find the Textual app entry point.
Find every Input widget and its submit handler in the source.
Check the pinned Textual version in the project file.
Create the plan file, then write the list of input IDs and handler names into it before any code change.
Run the existing test suite as a baseline and note the pass count.

K-018003.example: The search app has two Input widgets, id="query" and id="filter", both handled in src/app.py. The pin in pyproject.toml is textual==0.86.0, so the plan targets that version's API. pytest -q reports 12 passed before any change.
K-018003.check: rg prints one line per Input( and on_input_submitted match, grep prints the textual pin line, PLAN_LOADING.md lists exactly the input IDs that rg found, and pytest -q prints a pass count with exit code 0.
traps: Small models guess widget names instead of reading them from the source. Plan only for inputs that submit work. Read the pinned version first, since Textual APIs change between releases.
Skipping the baseline run means a later failure cannot be told apart from an existing one.

steps.do: Find any existing disabled flags in the source so the new rule matches them.
Write the rule into PLAN_LOADING.md: input.disabled is True while loading and False when loading ends, including the error case.
Count the submit handlers that can start work from this input.
Count lines in the main app file to size the change; a count above 400 means split the change into two files.
Run the test suite and confirm the pass count is unchanged by the plan-only step.

K-018004.example: The plan sets Input.disabled = True during loading so a second Enter is ignored. rg shows on_input_submitted once in src/app.py, so only one handler needs the change. wc -l prints 310, under the 400 limit, so one file is enough.
K-018004.check: rg prints one on_input_submitted line for src/app.py, wc -l prints a line count compared against the 400 threshold, and pytest -q prints a pass count with exit code 0.
traps: Blocking typing when the user should still see their text. Forgetting to re-enable the input on error. Assuming disabled removes focus automatically.

steps.do: Confirm the project uses Svelte 5, because the $props rune is required.
Find existing components that already use $props so you match the project style.
Write a TypeScript union type named TableStatus with the values loading, empty, error, and ready, and plan to read it with let { status } = $props().
Run svelte-check to confirm the planned types compile against the current code.

K-018005.example: npm ls svelte prints svelte@5.x, and svelte-check then reports 0 errors. A union of four literal strings gives the table exactly four status values to handle.
K-018005.check: npm ls svelte shows a version starting with 5, and npx svelte-check --threshold error ends with 0 errors.
traps: Small models use Svelte 4 export let syntax in Svelte 5 code. Use $props, not export let.
A plain string type lets any typo compile. Use the literal union so a missing state fails the type check.

steps.do: Check whether svelte:boundary is already used in the source tree.
Confirm the Svelte version is 5.3 or later, because svelte:boundary needs it.
Write in the plan that the boundary wraps only the table, and its failed snippet shows the error message and a retry button.
Count how many boundaries the plan adds, which should be one for the table.

K-018006.example: If npm ls svelte prints svelte@5.4.0, the boundary is available. The plan then has one boundary around the table, so grep -c prints 1.
K-018006.check: npm ls svelte prints a version of 5.3 or higher, and grep -c prints 1 for the table boundary in the plan.
traps: Small models expect svelte:boundary to catch errors from async fetches. It only catches render and effect errors, so fetch failures still need the error state.
Wrapping the whole page in one boundary replaces the table and its filters on any failure. Wrap only the table.

steps.do: Write in the plan one heading, one sentence of message, and one primary button for the empty state.
Write the minimum button height as 44px and the text contrast as 4.5:1 in the plan.
Count the empty-state elements the plan lists, which should be three: heading, message, and button.
After the component exists, run an accessibility scan on the page that shows the empty state.

K-018007.example: The plan lists heading, message, and button on three lines, so grep -c prints 3. After the build, npx axe on the empty route should report zero violations for contrast below 4.5:1.
K-018007.check: grep -c prints 3, and the later axe scan reports 0 violations for color-contrast.
traps: Small models give the empty state a second button for clearing filters. Keep one action unless the plan names a second one.
Small models set button padding with no minimum height, so the target can fall below 44px. Set min-height: 44px in the plan.

steps.do: Write in the plan that the spinner appears only after 200ms of loading, so fast loads do not flicker.
Write in the plan that a retry button re-runs the same data request and returns the table to loading.
Create the test file that will prove the loading delay and retry behavior.
List the test files that exist so you can confirm the new file is in the right folder.

K-018008.example: The plan sets the spinner delay at 200ms, and the test file tests/table-states.spec.ts appears in the ls output. Later, npx playwright test reports the retry test as passed.
K-018008.check: ls tests shows table-states.spec.ts, and the plan file names the 200ms delay and the retry behavior.
traps: Small models show the spinner at once, which causes flicker on fast loads. Use the 200ms delay in the plan.
Retry that does not clear the error message leaves stale text on screen. The plan must say retry resets the state to loading.

steps.do: Confirm the parent container already uses CSS grid or flexbox.
Plan the base layout as one column with no media query.
Plan the wider layout with a range query at 40rem, which is 640px at the default 16px root size.
Set the grid to auto-fit with minmax so columns wrap without a breakpoint.
Confirm the minimum column width is 16rem or wider so text does not squeeze.

K-018009.example: The empty state uses grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr)), so a 320px phone gets one column and a 1024px desktop gets three. The min(100%, 16rem) part keeps the column from ever exceeding its parent width.
K-018009.check: grep -n 'display: grid' prints at least one matching line, and the plan lists a 320px single-column case and a 1024px multi-column case.
traps: Using a fixed count like repeat(3, 1fr) breaks on phones. Leaving out min(100%, ...) lets a column overflow a narrow parent.

steps.do: Find out whether any ancestor already declares a container type.
Plan one wrapper with container-type set to inline-size.
Name the container so inner rules target it by name, for example empty-host.
Plan an @container rule at 28rem that switches the card from stacked to side-by-side.
Check whether any @container rules already exist in the stylesheet.

K-018010.example: The wrapper .panel-main sets container-type: inline-size, so a 360px sidebar keeps the stacked layout. A 720px main panel crosses the 28rem query and switches .empty-state to flex-direction: row.
K-018010.check: grep -rn 'container-type' prints the wrapper line with inline-size, and the plan names the query threshold as 28rem.
traps: container-type applies to the wrapper, not the card itself, so putting it on the card does not work. Using size instead of inline-size can collapse the element height.

steps.do: List each interactive element inside the empty state.
Set the minimum touch target to 44px height and 44px width for each element.
Set the body text to 1rem minimum so the user's font size preference is respected.
Plan the heading with clamp, for example clamp(1.25rem, 4vw, 2rem).
Confirm the planned heights against the existing min-height rules.

K-018011.example: The primary button uses min-height: 44px and padding: 0.75rem 1.25rem, and the heading uses font-size: clamp(1.25rem, 4vw, 2rem). That makes the heading 20px at a 320px viewport and 32px at an 800px viewport.
K-018011.check: grep -n 'min-height' shows a 44px value for the button rule, and the plan records a clamp minimum of 1.25rem.
traps: Using px for body text blocks the user's font size preference. A 44px target applies to the whole tappable box, not only the icon inside it.

steps.do: Check whether reduced-motion handling already exists in the stylesheet.
Record the text color and background color pair for the empty-state body text.
Confirm the body text contrast meets 4.5:1 against its background.
Plan a reduced-motion query that sets animation-duration to 0.01ms on the empty-state icon.
Plan the icon as decorative with aria-hidden set to true when it repeats the heading text.

K-018012.example: Body text #595959 on #ffffff gives a contrast ratio of about 7.0:1, well above 4.5:1. The icon bounce animation is disabled inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce).
K-018012.check: grep -rn 'prefers-reduced-motion' prints a match or nothing, and the plan lists a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for each text pair.
traps: Meeting 4.5:1 for the heading alone is not enough, so check every text pair. A reduced-motion query does not have to remove all motion, only the parts that move.

steps.do: Confirm Tailwind is installed in the project and note the version.
Add the select with the mobile width as the base class and the wider width behind the sm: prefix.
Rebuild the stylesheet so the sm: classes are generated.
Count the sm:w-auto uses in the markup to confirm the class is present.
Confirm the responsive width rule was emitted into the built CSS.

K-018013.example: <select class='w-full sm:w-auto sm:min-w-[16rem] rounded-md border-gray-300'> stays full width at 375px and becomes at least 16rem wide from 640px. The base class w-full applies at every size, and sm:w-auto overrides it only from the sm breakpoint up.
K-018013.check: grep -c sm:w-auto src/index.html prints 1 or more, and grep -c w-auto dist/output.css prints 1 or more.
traps: Writing sm:w-full where the base w-full was needed, because sm: applies upward from 640px and not downward.
Building class names by string concatenation such as sm:w-${size} produces no CSS, since Tailwind only generates classes it finds as literal text in the source.

steps.do: Check the installed Tailwind version so you know the text-base default.
Set the select to text-base on mobile and text-sm from the md breakpoint up.
Set a 44px minimum height on the select so it is a usable touch target.
Rebuild the stylesheet so text-base and min-h-[44px] are emitted.
Confirm the 1rem font size from text-base is present in the built CSS.

K-018014.example: <select class='w-full min-h-[44px] px-3 py-2 text-base md:text-sm'> renders at 16px on a 375px phone and 14px at 768px and up. The min-h-[44px] class keeps the control at least 44px tall for touch.
K-018014.check: grep -c 'font-size: 1rem' dist/output.css prints 1 or more, and the select element measures at least 44px tall at a 375px viewport.
traps: Using text-sm as the base class, which is 14px and triggers iOS zoom on focus.
Setting text-base but dropping md:text-sm, which leaves desktop text oversized.
A small model may also write min-h-[40px], which is below the 44px touch target.

steps.do: Install the Tailwind forms plugin that resets select styling.
Add appearance-none, a background chevron image sized 1rem, and right padding to the select.
Register the forms plugin in the stylesheet with the plugin directive, which is the Tailwind v4 form.
Build the stylesheet so appearance-none and the background utilities are emitted.
Confirm the appearance rule exists in the built CSS.

K-018015.example: <select class='appearance-none bg-[url(/chevron.svg)] bg-[length:1rem] bg-[right_0.75rem_center] bg-no-repeat w-full pr-10 sm:pr-12'> places the chevron 0.75rem from the right edge and adds more padding from 640px. The pr-10 class reserves room so option text does not run under the arrow.
K-018015.check: grep -c appearance dist/output.css prints 1 or more, and the built CSS contains appearance: none for the select.
traps: Omitting appearance-none, so the native arrow stacks on top of the custom chevron.
Setting pr-10 on a narrow phone layout where the label overlaps the arrow at 320px, so the padding must be checked at small widths too.

steps.do: Wrap the label and select in a container with a column layout as the base and a row layout from md.
Give the label a fixed width only from md so the select fills the remaining space.
Add min-w-0 to the select so long option text truncates instead of pushing the row wider than the screen.
Rebuild the stylesheet so the flex and md: classes are emitted.
Count the rows that use the md:flex-row class in the markup.

K-018016.example: <div class='flex flex-col gap-2 md:flex-row md:items-center'><label class='shrink-0 md:w-40'>Region</label><select class='w-full min-w-0 md:flex-1'> stacks at 375px and places the label beside the select from 768px. The shrink-0 class stops the label from squeezing, and md:flex-1 lets the select take the remaining width.
K-018016.check: grep -c md:flex-row src/index.html prints the number of form rows, for example 3 for three rows, and the layout is a single column at 375px in the browser.
traps: Writing flex-row as the base and flex-col at md, which reverses the mobile stacking.
Leaving out shrink-0 on the label, so it compresses on tablets, or writing w-40 without the md: prefix, which makes the label wide on phones too.

steps.do: Wrap the selects in a grid with one column as the explicit base.
Add sm:grid-cols-2 and lg:grid-cols-3 so the columns widen with the viewport.
Set gap-4 so the spacing is the same at every breakpoint.
Rebuild the stylesheet in minified form.
List each grid-cols class found in the markup to confirm all three breakpoints are present.

K-018017.example: <div class='grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3'> holds six selects that show one per row at 375px, two per row at 640px, and three per row at 1024px. The explicit grid-cols-1 base keeps the phone layout defined rather than left to the browser default.
K-018017.check: grep -o grid-cols-[0-9] src/index.html prints three lines: grid-cols-1, grid-cols-2, and grid-cols-3.
traps: Setting grid-cols-3 as the base, which squeezes selects below 320px.
Leaving out the grid-cols-1 base and relying on the default, which makes the phone layout unclear to anyone who reads the markup.

steps.do: Mark the parent wrapper as a container with the container class.
Apply the @sm variant to widen the select once the container reaches 24rem.
Build the stylesheet with the Tailwind v4 CLI package.
Confirm a container query rule was emitted into the built CSS.
Confirm the sidebar markup uses no viewport sm: width classes on this select.

K-018018.example: <div class='@container'><select class='w-full @sm:w-64 rounded-md'> stays full width inside a 280px sidebar and becomes 16rem wide once the container is at least 24rem. The @sm variant reads the parent width, so the same select behaves correctly in a narrow sidebar at any viewport size.
K-018018.check: grep -c @container dist/output.css prints 1 or more, and grep -c sm:w- src/sidebar.html prints 0.
traps: Using the viewport sm: prefix, which widens the select at 640px even when the sidebar is only 200px wide.
Forgetting the container class on the parent, so @sm has no effect, or writing sm without the @ symbol, which is the wrong variant form.

steps.do: List every file that mentions an empty state by class name.
Record the line numbers where the empty-state rules live in the stylesheet.
Count the media queries already in the stylesheet so you reuse existing breakpoints.
Count how many empty-state lines set a 44px touch target, so you know the existing sizing baseline.
Write down each distinct breakpoint value found, in rem or px, as a list.

K-018019.example: grep -rln reports index.html and styles.css, grep -c '@media' returns 3, and grep -c '44px' returns 2. The plan keeps the existing breakpoints of 30rem, 48rem and 64rem, and reuses the 44px touch target instead of adding a new size.
K-018019.check: grep -c '@media' prints a count of 1 or more, each matched file path is listed, the 44px count is a number of 0 or more, and the planned breakpoint list has the same number of entries as the @media count.
traps: Small models often invent new breakpoints without checking the stylesheet first. Searching one file misses markup in templates or partials. Counting @media lines is not the same as counting distinct …

steps.do: Confirm the docs folder exists before writing the plan.
Create the docs folder if the listing reports it missing.
Create the empty plan file so the build stage has a fixed path.
Write the breakpoint, grid, container, and sizing decisions into that file as a short list with units on every value.
Confirm the plan file exists and is not empty.
Count the decision lines in the file so none are missing.
Confirm the plan records the 44px touch target as a number, with a count of 1 or more.

K-018020.example: The file docs/empty-state-responsive-plan.md lists breakpoints 40rem and 64rem, a 44px touch target, and a 16rem grid minimum. wc -l reports 8 lines, and grep -c '44px' reports 1, which covers the four decision groups and the touch target.
K-018020.check: stat prints a file size above 0 bytes, wc -l prints a count of at least 4 for the four decision groups, and grep -c '44px' prints a count of 1 or more.
traps: Writing the plan only in chat leaves the build stage with nothing to read. A value without a unit, such as 40 instead of 40rem, causes errors when the build stage uses it.

steps.do: Enter the ratatui project directory that holds Cargo.toml.
Confirm the ratatui version pinned in Cargo.toml is 0.29 or newer.
Check that the test file builds TestBackend at 80 by 24 and at 40 by 12.
Run only the responsive layout tests in the layout test target.
Run the full suite once to catch regressions in other widgets.

K-018021.example: At width 80 the sidebar Rect has width 24 and the list fills the rest, while at width 40 the sidebar stacks above the list with width 40. The asserts compare area.width against the constants 24 and 40 from the test file.
K-018021.check: The responsive run prints 'test result: ok. 2 passed' and grep prints two lines, one with TestBackend::new(80, 24) and one with TestBackend::new(40, 12).
traps: Testing only the 80-column case leaves the stacked branch unproven.
Ratatui Rect x and y start at 0, so checking x equal to 1 fails for the first column.
A println of the layout without an assert passes even when the widths are wrong.

steps.do: Enter the ratatui project directory.
Find the constant that sets the wide layout threshold.
Run the test that renders at width 79 and expects the compact layout.
Run the test that renders at width 80 and expects the wide layout.
Read the comparison in src to confirm it uses greater-or-equal to the constant.

K-018022.example: WIDE_MIN is 80, so a terminal 79 columns wide picks the compact branch and 80 columns picks the wide branch. Each test builds a TestBackend of exactly that width and checks which widgets are present in the buffer.
K-018022.check: Both cargo test runs print 'test result: ok. 1 passed', and grep prints a line like pub const WIDE_MIN: u16 = 80.
traps: Testing only width 80 misses a comparison written as greater-than instead of greater-or-equal.
Treating the 79 case as proof of the 80 case skips the boundary itself.
Using a width from a real terminal instead of a fixed TestBackend makes the boundary result change between machines.

steps.do: Enter the Textual project directory.
Install the test dependencies from the requirements file.
Run the narrow test that sets the app size to 60 by 20.
Run the wide test that sets the app size to 120 by 40.
Confirm the tests assert on widget region width and not only on rendering.

K-018023.example: Inside async with app.run_test(size=(60, 20)) as pilot, the #sidebar widget is hidden so its region.width is 0. Under size=(120, 40) the same widget has region.width 30 after await pilot.pause().
K-018023.check: Both pytest runs print '1 passed' with exit code 0, and grep prints at least two lines containing region.width.
traps: Calling run_test with no size uses the default 80 by 24 and proves nothing about other sizes.
Reading region before await pilot.pause() returns values from the previous layout pass.
A test that only checks the app starts does not prove the panels resized.

steps.do: Enter the ratatui project directory.
Find where the minimum size constants are defined.
Run the test that renders at 20 by 5 and expects the fallback text.
Run the test that renders at exactly the minimum size and expects the normal widgets.
Confirm the fallback test asserts the literal text instead of only checking for no panic.

K-018024.example: A TestBackend of 20 by 5 has the text 'too small' in its buffer and no Block border cells. At the exact minimum of 40 by 12 the buffer has the border corner symbol at position (0, 0).
K-018024.check: Both cargo test runs print 'test result: ok. 1 passed', and grep prints at least one line containing too small.
traps: Checking only that the program does not panic passes even when the screen is blank.
Using minimum minus one as the test width makes a boundary check pass for the wrong reason.
Comparing the buffer against a string without trimming trailing spaces causes false mismatches.

steps.do: Search the table component for hex color literals.
Run ESLint on the table component to catch color rule violations.
Type-check the project so the theme token types compile.

K-018025.example: The search should return zero matches for a table styled with var(--table-bg) and var(--table-fg). ESLint should report 0 errors and tsc should exit with code 0.
K-018025.check: rg prints nothing and exits with code 1, eslint prints no errors, and tsc exits with code 0 and no output.
traps: Colors can hide in inline style props such as style={{ color: '#fff' }}, so search every component file, not only CSS.
A search that prints nothing is a pass here, not an error.
Also search for rgb() and hsl() literals, not just hex.

steps.do: Confirm the dev server answers on port 5173 before running the test.
Run the Playwright spec that toggles the theme and reads computed colors.
If the test fails, read the assertion diff to see which color value was wrong.

K-018026.example: After clicking the theme toggle, the spec expects the header cell background to equal rgb(18, 18, 18) in dark mode and rgb(255, 255, 255) in light mode. The run should finish with one passing test.
K-018026.check: curl returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK and Playwright prints '1 passed' with no failed assertions.
traps: A 404 from curl means the route is wrong, not that the theme is broken.
Read computed styles with getComputedStyle, because the CSS source file can show a value that never applies.
Wait for the theme attribute to change before reading colors, or the test will read stale values.

steps.do: Confirm the dark theme page loads before running the accessibility scan.
Scan the dark theme table page with axe for WCAG 2 AA rules and fail on any violation.
Check the axe output for any color-contrast entries.

K-018027.example: Body text in the table should have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background, and header text at least 4.5:1 too. The axe scan should report no color-contrast violations.
K-018027.check: curl returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK, and the axe command exits with code 0 with no color-contrast violations listed.
traps: Axe checks only rendered DOM, so colors applied after a user action, such as hover or selected rows, need their own scan.
Normal text needs 4.5:1, while large bold text needs only 3:1.
Do not claim a pass if axe was not run on the dark route.

steps.do: Run the Vitest suite for the theme provider.
Confirm the table component reads the theme through the hook.
Type-check the project to confirm the context value type matches its consumers.

K-018028.example: The provider test should render a consumer, call setTheme('dark'), and assert that the consumer shows 'dark'. The table file should contain at least one import of useTheme.
K-018028.check: Vitest prints 'Test Files 1 passed' and 'Tests 3 passed', rg prints a line number for useTheme, and tsc exits with code 0.
traps: A provider test that never renders a consumer proves nothing about the table.
Check that the default context value is not silently used when the provider is missing.
Vitest needs a DOM environment such as jsdom, or render calls will fail.

steps.do: Count how many table theme variables the table stylesheet uses.
Confirm the global stylesheet declares color-scheme for both themes.
Check that the table stylesheet passes Prettier formatting.

K-018029.example: The table stylesheet should use at least 6 table variables, such as --table-bg, --table-fg, --table-border, --table-stripe, --table-hover, and --table-header. The global file should contain a line like color-scheme: light dark.
K-018029.check: rg prints a count of 6 or more for the stylesheet, rg prints a line containing 'color-scheme: light dark', and Prettier prints 'All matched files use Prettier code style!'.
traps: A count of zero can mean the variable prefix changed, not that the table lacks theming.
A color-scheme line set only to light will leave native scrollbars and form controls in the wrong theme.
Prettier only checks format, not whether the colors are correct.

steps.do: Confirm the dev server is up before timing the toggle.
Run the Playwright spec that times the theme toggle with performance.now.
Check whether the table rows are memoized so a theme change does not re-render every row.

K-018030.example: The spec records performance.now() before the toggle click and after the header background changes, then expects the difference to be less than 200ms. A memo call on the row component should appear in DataTable.tsx.
K-018030.check: curl returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK, Playwright prints '1 passed', and rg prints at least one line that uses memo.
traps: Timing a click without waiting for the new color can report a time that is too short.
Timings vary between runs, so run the spec several times and use the slowest result.
A memo on the table alone does not stop row re-renders if the row props change every render.

steps.do: Open src/ui/chart.rs and find the draw_chart function that builds the Chart widget.
Add an early return before Chart::new that renders a centered Paragraph reading No data when the data slice is empty, still drawing the outer Block border.
Add tests/chart_states.rs with a test named chart_empty_renders_placeholder that draws into TestBackend::new(40, 10).
Run only the empty-state test.

K-018031.example: An empty Vec of points makes draw_chart render Paragraph::new("No data") centered in a 40x10 area. The test asserts the buffer text contains No data and that Chart is never constructed.
K-018031.check: cargo test prints test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored.
traps: Small models often pass zero points to Chart and assume it shows a message, but ratatui only draws empty axes. A filter that matches no test name also exits 0 with 0 passed, so confirm the output say…
Do not return early before drawing the Block, or the panel border disappears.

steps.do: Search src/ui for existing Paragraph widgets so the new error panel matches their style.
Add the ChartState::Error(msg) arm that renders Paragraph::new(msg.as_str()) with fg Color::Red inside Block::bordered titled Error.
Enable Wrap with trim set to true so long messages wrap inside the area.
Add a test chart_error_shows_message in tests/chart_states.rs that draws Error("timeout") into TestBackend::new(40, 6).
Run the error-state test.

K-018032.example: Error("fetch timed out after 5s") renders in red inside a bordered block on a 40x6 test backend. The test asserts the buffer contains the word timed out.
K-018032.check: cargo test prints test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed.
traps: Red text alone fails for users who cannot see color, so keep the word Error in the block title. An empty error string draws a blank box, so substitute a default message.
terminal.draw returns a Result, so do not call unwrap on it without a reason.

steps.do: Find where the Axis bounds are computed in src/ui/chart.rs.
Add pub fn safe_bounds(min: f64, max: f64) -> [f64; 2] that returns [min - 1.0, max + 1.0] when min equals max and [min, max] otherwise.
Use safe_bounds for both the x and y Axis.
Add a #[cfg(test)] module at the bottom of src/ui/chart.rs with a test named axis_bounds_single_point asserting safe_bounds(5.0, 5.0) equals [4.0, 6.0].
Run that test.

K-018033.example: A single point at (5.0, 5.0) would give bounds [5.0, 5.0], so safe_bounds returns [4.0, 6.0] and the axis keeps a visible range. Empty data never reaches this function.
K-018033.check: cargo test prints test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed.
traps: Equal min and max give a zero-width axis, which can cause a divide-by-zero in scaling. Empty data has no min or max, so call safe_bounds only after checking the data is non-empty.
A fixed pad of 1.0 is too large for values near 0.001, so consider scaling the pad to the magnitude of the data.
